cards.title: Excluding one-sided randomized quasilinear-time log-space SAT
cards.formal:
Is it true that no uniform randomized random-access algorithm decides Boolean satisfiability with one-sided error while using both quasilinear time and logarithmic workspace? More precisely, for every integer \(k\ge0\), is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{RTISP}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k,\ \log_2(N+2)\right]?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length. The two bounds hold simultaneously for one machine on every input and every sequence of coin flips. The error is allowed only on satisfiable inputs: each is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), whereas an unsatisfiable input is never accepted.
cards.why: This asks whether the known obstruction to extremely fast, very low-memory SAT algorithms survives useful one-sided randomness. An unconditional answer would advance lower bounds for a central NP-complete problem in a general computation model.

The checked randomized results concern the opposite error direction or larger quantified/verification classes. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution of this exact randomized SAT target; this is not an exhaustive literature or independent proof certification.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary explicitly written satisfiability instance.
A candidate algorithm may use fresh random bits, logarithmic working memory and time n times a fixed polynomial in log n.
It must never accept an unsatisfiable formula and must accept each satisfiable formula with constant probability.
Both resource bounds hold for the same machine on every sequence of random choices.
The target is an unconditional lower bound against every such algorithm; known opposite-error and larger-class results do not settle it.

cards.definitions:
An input is an explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula: a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most three literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. The empty clause is false and the empty conjunction is true. An assignment gives a Boolean value to every variable occurring; the formula is satisfiable when some assignment makes it true. Variable identifiers, signs, all occurrences and clause delimiters are written in a fixed self-delimiting binary list encoding. Identifiers can be taken from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused identifiers permitted; \(N\) counts bits, not variables or clauses. Malformed encodings are no instances. There is no compressed formula or promise on the formula’s structure. The source explicitly permits 3-CNF satisfiability as its SAT target.

For definiteness, a random-access machine is a finite Turing-machine program with ordinary finite-alphabet work tapes and an address tape. When the address tape contains a binary index, one query step reads that indexed input bit; an out-of-range index returns a fixed endmarker. Writing, modifying and storing an address are charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only; all work tapes start blank. The total number of distinct work-tape cells visited, including the address tape and all temporary counters, is the workspace. This permits unrestricted repeated input access without charging the distance between input positions. Work-tape access uses ordinary moves. With only logarithmic work storage, the usual random-access work-memory or logarithmic-word variants can be simulated with polynomial-logarithmic time overhead and logarithmic space, so this quasilinear-time union is unchanged. There is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers, advice, oracle, external storage or extra catalytic tape.

At a random step the machine receives one fresh independent unbiased bit, at unit time cost. The random stream is available only in order and cannot be reread unless the machine stores the desired bits in its charged workspace. A random step is not a query to a random-access tape of reusable random bits. The machine eventually outputs accept or reject, without needing to output an assignment.

Write \(\ell_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Membership in the displayed RTISP class would mean that one fixed machine and positive integer constants \(C,D\) satisfy, on every input and every random stream,
\[\text{time}\le T_N=D(N+2)\ell_N^k,\qquad \text{visited work cells}\le C\ell_N.\]
The harmless \(N+2\) makes the bound total at small lengths. Constants and \(k\) may depend on the machine, but not on the formula. In particular, this is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time or high-probability resource guarantee. At most \(T_N\) random bits can be consumed. Acceptance probability can therefore be defined as the fraction of strings in \(\{0,1\}^{T_N}\) that make the machine accept, ignoring unused trailing bits. For every valid satisfiable formula this fraction is at least \(2/3\); for every unsatisfiable or malformed input it is zero. A fixed positive success constant in place of \(2/3\) is equivalent by a constant number of repetitions, preserving the resource form and error direction.

The conjecture quantifies over every fixed \(k,C,D\) and every finite program. It concerns the simultaneous time-and-space class: a fast algorithm with large memory and a separate slow logarithmic-space algorithm would not supply the forbidden machine. The randomness is internal to the algorithm; inputs are arbitrary, not drawn from a specified distribution.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated nonexistence claim. A positive answer must exclude every uniform randomized machine, every fixed logarithmic-space constant, and every fixed polynomial-logarithmic time factor, with the specified one-way coins and error direction. A negative answer must give one machine and fixed \(k,C,D\), prove its time and space bounds on every random branch, and prove zero acceptance on no instances and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes instance. Bounds for deterministic machines, the opposite one-sided error, quantified formulas with extra quantifier alternations, a selected family of SAT solvers or expected resource usage do not establish this assertion. Neither an unproved separation such as P ≠ NP nor a conditional lower bound settles the unconditional target. The conclusion and probabilities have their exact stated meanings; no numerical approximation tolerance applies.

context_blocks.text: Randomized search for a satisfying assignment may miss an assignment that exists, while an accepted assignment can be checked for correctness. This motivates the source’s error direction. The target nevertheless ranges over all decision algorithms with this error behavior, not just procedures that explicitly search for or output an assignment.

Logarithmic memory holds only a small number of indices and counters. The input can be read repeatedly, but the time bound permits only a polynomial-logarithmic amount of overhead beyond its length. Randomness supplies fresh choices without furnishing free reusable storage. All three features—input access, memory and access to coins—matter.

Diehl and van Melkebeek prove polynomial-strength randomized lower bounds for quantified Boolean formulas with at least two quantifier blocks. Their theorem’s restriction excludes plain existential satisfiability. Higher-level quantified formulas cannot simply be substituted for the SAT instances in this card.

Their one-sided lower bound for tautology yields a bound for SAT with the opposite permitted error: always accept a satisfiable formula, but possibly accept an unsatisfiable one. Complementing outputs switches both the language and the error side. It does not yield the requested lower bound for algorithms that never accept an unsatisfiable input.

The 2016 source explains why ordinary space-efficient derandomization does not already settle the question. Its polynomial running-time overhead is too large for the known deterministic time-space lower bounds to contradict the resulting SAT algorithm. A qualitative polynomial-time simulation does not preserve the near-linear time requirement.

The 2021 paper extends time-space lower bounds to problems with randomized or quantum verification. Its Main Theorem 3 concerns linear-time Merlin–Arthur and quantum Merlin–Arthur classes against randomized logarithmic-space machines. Such a verifier receives an additional proposed witness; lower bounds for those larger classes are not automatically lower bounds for SAT.

cards.title: Real quantifier alternation versus summation
cards.formal: For every fixed \(t\ge1\), does the truth problem for closed real-arithmetic sentences with at most \(t\) alternating quantifier blocks admit a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\), the existential theory of the reals with Boolean summation binders? Equivalently, is every fixed level of the real polynomial hierarchy contained in \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) as defined below? The polynomial-time reduction and its degree may depend on \(t\); the number of real variables in each block is unrestricted. Either existential or universal first blocks are included.
cards.why: Alternating real quantifiers express geometric and optimization conditions beyond pure existence. Finite summation over Boolean choices adds a form of counting without introducing new real quantifier blocks. Comparing these resources would clarify whether a single strengthened existential theory captures all fixed levels of the real hierarchy.
cards.status_note: Open in the checked ISAAC 2024 Section 9 and its full preprint. The earlier Basu–Zell topological theorem has a different target, while later corrections to bounded-domain real hierarchies do not prove this unrestricted summation containment. Bounded subsequent-result checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

cards.definitions:
The source input is a closed prenex sentence \(Q_1X_1\cdots Q_sX_s\,\phi\), where \(0\le s\le t\), each \(X_j\) is a finite tuple of distinct real variables, consecutive \(Q_j\in\{\exists,\forall\}\) differ, and every quantified variable ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\). There are no free variables. The matrix \(\phi\) is a finite Boolean formula using \(\land,\lor,\neg\) and comparisons \(u=v\), \(u<v\), or \(u\le v\). Its arithmetic terms are finite expression trees built from integer constants, variables, binary addition, subtraction and multiplication. Integers are encoded by a sign and ordinary binary magnitude; variable indices are binary integers. Fix a parenthesized prefix encoding over a finite alphabet for all tree nodes, operators, variable indices and tuple lists. Input size is the full bit length of this encoding. There is no shared-subexpression circuit, implicit large power, summation binder or succinct indexing in these source terms. Binary integer constants and subtraction can equivalently be expressed using the source papers’ constants \(0,1\) and ring operations with polynomial overhead.

A target \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\) instance is a closed sentence \(\exists y_1\cdots\exists y_m\,\psi\), where \(m\ge0\), \(\psi\) is a Boolean formula of the same comparisons, and its arithmetic expression trees additionally allow the binder \(\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}}u\). This denotes \(u[b:=0]+u[b:=1]\). The bound symbol \(b\) is a local dummy scalar variable, distinct from the existentially quantified real variables and from other active dummy variables; usual capture-free substitution fixes its semantics. Binders may be nested, and their body is stored once, so nesting can describe exponentially many summands. All free variables in terms must be among the explicitly listed \(y_j\) or in scope of a summation binder. A dummy value may occur as a number in a term but cannot select a variable name: an expression such as \(y_b\), with a value-dependent index, is forbidden. No product binder, Boolean-formula binder, arbitrary real constant, real exponentiation, extra real quantifier alternation or succinct circuit representation is allowed. The size counts the finite syntax including each binder and its body, rather than the fully expanded sum. Thus the number of distinct existential real variables is at most the target length.

A deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction is a single finite-program multitape Turing machine that, on each valid input string of length \(L\), outputs one valid target sentence within \(C_t(L+1)^{c_t}\) bit transitions and preserves truth in both directions. It uses no random bits, advice, real-arithmetic oracle or decision oracle. Output length and all construction work count. Constants \(C_t,c_t\) and the machine may depend on the fixed block bound \(t\), but not on a particular input. The target class \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) consists of binary-string languages polynomial-time many-one reducible to truth of these target sentences. The real polynomial hierarchy here is the union of the analogous closures of the source truth problems over all fixed \(t\). Its definition does not allow the block bound to grow with the input length.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof providing a truth-preserving polynomial-time reduction for every fixed block bound \(t\), or a complete Lean proof that such a reduction fails for at least one fixed \(t\). The affirmative proof must respect the target’s explicit variable list and summation-only syntax. A PSPACE upper bound, a reduction to a language with product binders or exponentially indexed real variables, or a reduction to a topological counting oracle is insufficient by itself.

context_blocks.text: The source’s phrase “real version of Toda’s theorem” is followed by the precise question of containment in \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\). This card uses that containment as its sole target. It does not ask for an unspecified analogue among other real-computation models.

The crucial target restriction is the absence of value-dependent variable indexing. The source distinguishes ordinary \(\Sigma\)-ETR from a stronger summation language capable of addressing exponentially many real variables.

The source proves that the summation class lies in PSPACE and contains ordinary existential real feasibility. By contrast, adding the corresponding compact product binder yields PSPACE-completeness. These bounds do not settle whether summation alone contains all fixed alternation levels.

Schaefer and Štefankovič define the discrete real hierarchy through truth of finitely encoded sentences and polynomial-time reductions. Their March 2025 revision corrects certain bounded-closed-domain claims. The present target uses unrestricted real domains and the full comparison signature, so it does not rely on the withdrawn bounded-domain equivalences.

Basu and Zell already proved a real analogue of Toda’s theorem using topological counting, namely Betti-number information, in a compact real-machine setting. That established theorem has a different oracle and model from the summation-only containment posed in 2024.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) perfect matching
cards.formal:
Does perfect-matching decision for general undirected graphs have nonuniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and logarithmic depth?

For each integer \(v\ge2\), let \(\mathrm{PM}_v:\{0,1\}^{\binom v2}\to\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the encoded graph has a perfect matching. The target is the existence of fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\) and circuits \((C_v)_{v\ge2}\) such that
\[\forall v\ge2,\quad |C_v|\le a(v+1)^b,\qquad\operatorname{depth}(C_v)\le d\lceil\log_2(v+2)\rceil,\]
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{\binom v2},\qquad C_v(x)=\mathrm{PM}_v(x).\]
The gates have fan-in at most two, and negation is allowed. The circuits need not be generated uniformly, and the output is only the decision bit.
cards.why: Perfect matching is a central polynomial-time graph problem whose exact bounded-fan-in depth remains poorly understood. A negative answer would separate nonuniform NC-one from P/poly using a concrete polynomial-time task. A positive answer would put the decision problem at a much shallower level than the broad polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithms studied in most matching work.

cards.definitions:
A graph has vertex set \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and an arbitrary set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices as edges. It is simple, undirected and unweighted, with no promise of bipartiteness, planarity, bounded degree or a matching already known to exist. Its input bits are \(x_{ij}\) for \(1\le i<j\le v\), in lexicographic order; \(x_{ij}=1\) precisely when the edge is present. Every bit string of this length is a valid graph. The input length \(m=\binom v2\) is polynomially related to \(v\), so the polynomial-size and logarithmic-depth requirements have the same meaning with either parameter. The statement starts at \(v=2\); the fixed zero- and one-vertex cases do not affect the asymptotic question.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to exactly one selected edge. Consequently \(\mathrm{PM}_v=0\) for odd \(v\). The algorithmic target is to output one bit indicating existence, not to construct a matching, count matchings or decide a weighted exact-value variant.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with variable inputs, constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. A gate output can feed arbitrarily many later gates. The size \(|C|\) is the number of computational gates, and depth is the maximum number of such gates on a path to the output. Variable and constant inputs have depth zero and do not count toward size. Input handling here is entirely through the indicated input wires; no oracle, random bits, threshold gates or unbounded-fan-in AND/OR primitives are present. Correctness is exact on every assignment.

Nonuniform means that each \(C_v\) may be chosen independently; there is no computability, logspace generation or polynomial-time construction requirement on the sequence. The integers \(a,b,d\) must nevertheless be fixed across all graph orders. This is the usual nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) target. A circuit satisfying the logarithmic depth bound can be expanded into a tree of polynomial size, so the simultaneous size requirement causes no additional asymptotic restriction in this single-output bounded-fan-in setting.

Equivalently, \(\mathrm{PM}_v\) must have polynomial-size De Morgan formulas. Such a formula is a rooted tree of binary AND/OR gates with possibly negated variable leaves; each repeated occurrence of a variable is counted separately, and internal values cannot be shared. Formula balancing yields logarithmic depth from polynomial leaf size. A negative answer is failure of every polynomial formula bound for this fixed family, or equivalently that its minimum circuit depth is not \(O(\log v)\); a lower bound may be witnessed at arbitrarily large graph orders rather than at every order.

For source fidelity, the draft’s function \(\mathrm{Match}_v\) asks whether the maximum matching size is at least \(v/3+1\), interpreted as the integer threshold \(k_v=\lceil v/3+1\rceil\). The two decision families are equivalent for the present circuit class. To express a size-at-least-\(k\) question as perfect matching, when \(0\le k\le v/2\), add \(v-2k\) new vertices adjacent to every original vertex and to no new vertex. The enlarged graph has a perfect matching exactly when the original graph has a matching of size at least \(k\). Thresholds above \(\lfloor v/2\rfloor\) are constantly false. Conversely, for a graph on \(2q\) vertices with \(q\ge3\), adding \(q-3\) isolated vertices makes the source threshold \((3q-3)/3+1=q\), so its Match answer is exactly the original perfect-matching answer. Smaller graph orders and odd perfect-matching orders have fixed finite answers. These transformations copy input bits and add fixed adjacency bits with only linear growth in vertex count, and hence preserve the nonuniform logarithmic-depth question in both directions.

A negative answer must prove that no such family exists, equivalently that perfect matching has no polynomial-size De Morgan formula family. cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), stable ternary compaction \(S_n:\{0,1,2\}^n\to\{0,1,2\}^n\) is computable by a Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates? The function deletes all symbols \(2\), retains all symbols \(0,1\) in their original relative order, and appends the deleted number of \(2\)s on the right. Circuits use the binary alphabet encoding and bounded-fan-in basis specified below, with no depth or uniformity restriction.
cards.definitions: Encode symbols \(0,1,2\) by \(00,01,10\), respectively, using a fixed ordered pair of bits for each input position. A circuit for length \(n\) is a finite acyclic directed Boolean circuit with \(2n\) ordered input bits and \(2n\) ordered output bits. Its non-input gates are binary AND, binary OR, unary NOT and optional constant-0 or constant-1 gates. Each such gate, including a constant gate, contributes one to size. Fan-out is unrestricted. Wires and output designations have no separate cost, and the same gate or input can feed multiple gates and outputs. The circuit is deterministic. It must be correct on every concatenation of valid input encodings; behavior on any input containing a pair \(11\) is unrestricted. For \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{0,1,2\}^n\), let \(i_1<\cdots<i_m\) be exactly the indices where \(a_i\ne2\). The required output encodes \(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m}\) followed by \(n-m\) copies of \(2\). This definition includes \(m=0\) and \(m=n\). In particular, it preserves the relative order of a \(0\) and a \(1\); it does not sort them against each other. All output positions must be produced by one circuit and their gates are counted jointly. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum permitted circuit size for this promise function. The quantifiers are \(\exists C\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\exists\mathcal C_n\), with \(|\mathcal C_n|\le Cn\) and exact correctness on all valid inputs. The circuit may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and no algorithm constructing \(\mathcal C_n\) is required. The circuit may compute on the individual encoding bits; it is not restricted to comparing or routing indivisible records.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(s(n)\le Cn\) for some universal \(C\) and all \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation \(\forall C\ge1\;\exists n\ge1,\ s(n)>Cn\). The negative statement rules out every nonuniform family in the defined unrestricted Boolean model; a lower bound for comparators or indivisible-record routing does not suffice. A conditional result under an additional conjecture settles only that conditional version. A positive answer must retain the original order of the \(0\)s and \(1\)s, with an exact linear size bound rather than a bound multiplied by an unbounded iterated-logarithm factor.
cards.why: This is an elementary deterministic rearrangement whose output preserves an arbitrary binary subsequence. Its sequential simplicity contrasts with the difficulty of arranging all output bits in a fixed circuit. Resolving linear circuit size would sharpen the boundary between data movement with input-dependent access and unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean computation.

importance.reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.

cards.title: KRW formula-size conjecture with constant loss
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(\alpha>0\) such that for every pair of positive integers \(n,m\) and every pair of nonconstant total Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), \(g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\),
\[L(g\circ f)\ge\alpha L(g)L(f)?\]
Here \((g\circ f)(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=g(f(x^{(1)}),\ldots,f(x^{(m)}))\) on \(m\) disjoint \(n\)-bit blocks, and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size. The constant is chosen before all dimensions and functions.

This card retains the constant-factor formula-size version displayed as Conjecture 5.13 in the source book. It is stronger than versions permitting a growing multiplicative loss. The original KRW paper formulates a depth-composition question; the card does not identify that question, weakened quantitative versions, and the displayed constant-loss formula statement as equivalent.
cards.why: A formula for a composition can substitute an inner computation wherever an outer input is used, multiplying the leaf counts. A universal matching lower bound would show that alternative Boolean factorizations cannot save more than a constant factor on arbitrary block compositions. This is a strong structural statement about formulas, closely connected to the source’s superpolynomial formula lower-bound question.

A bounded later-work search did not identify a proof or refutation of this exact all-function constant-loss formula-size version. Its strong quantitative choice follows the book’s display and is distinguished from the original depth question and relaxed KRW variants. cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(r\), a total Boolean function is a map \(h:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\). Nonconstant means that it takes both values on its domain; it need not depend on every designated input coordinate. A De Morgan formula for \(h\) is a finite rooted tree whose internal operations are binary AND, binary OR, and unary NOT, and whose leaves are input variables or the constant bits zero and one. Its value is obtained by the usual Boolean operations from leaves to the root. It must compute \(h\) exactly on every input, with no randomness or promise on input values. There are no parity, threshold, arbitrary truth-table or unbounded-fan-in gates.

Formula size is the number of occurrences of input variables among its leaves. Positive and negated occurrences both count, and different occurrences of the same variable count separately. Constant leaves are free and can be eliminated from an optimum for a nonconstant function. NOT operations can be pushed onto variables without changing this measure. The minimum over all such formulas is \(L(h)\); it is a finite positive integer for nonconstant \(h\). No internal value can be shared between two parent operations: such reuse would produce a circuit rather than a formula.

The composed function has exactly \(mn\) designated coordinates \(x^{(j)}_i\), with \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Block coordinates are distinct and unconstrained. The same inner function \(f\) is applied to every block, and its outputs, in block order, become the inputs of \(g\). The composition symbol here means this block operation, not ordinary composition of two maps with the same domain. Both functions and their composition may be specified by arbitrary finite truth tables, and no uniformity, polynomial-time evaluability, or monotonicity is assumed.

Since both functions are nonconstant, every Boolean vector supplied to \(g\) can be realized by some collection of blocks, and the composition is nonconstant. The usual substitution bound gives \(L(g\circ f)\le L(g)L(f)\). The question is whether the ratio to that upper bound is bounded away from zero uniformly over all functions and dimensions. Equivalently, is the infimum of these positive ratios strictly positive? This infimum need not be attained. Restricting \(0<\alpha\le1\) is equivalent.

The negation says that for every positive \(\alpha\), some pair and dimensions have ratio smaller than \(\alpha\). Thus a single saving relative to exact multiplication, or even failure of one proposed constant, is insufficient to refute the claim. Allowing constant functions with the convention \(L(h)=0\) would add only trivial inequalities; their exclusion makes the ratio formulation well-defined. Minimum depth, which counts gates along a longest path, is a different measure from the number of leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the constant-loss formula-size statement. A positive answer must establish one strictly positive factor for every permitted pair and dimensions. A negative answer must establish ratios arbitrarily close to zero, not merely a finite violation of equality or an unbounded additive saving in formula depth. Bounds for almost all functions, for special inner functions, for monotone formulas, or for a stronger communication search task do not alone prove the all-function claim. A composition inequality with a loss depending on either dimension, even polylogarithmically, is a weaker result unless upgraded to the fixed constant required here.

Those depth examples are not, by themselves, counterexamples to a constant-factor statement about minimum formula leaf count. The original paper and the later size formulation must be distinguished.

The 2023 paper explicitly distinguishes the original depth conjecture from the formula-size variant. cards.definitions:
An instance is \(I=(n,o,s_0,s_1)\), where \(n\ge1\), the ordinary vertices are \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(o\in V\) is the origin, and \(d_0,d_1\notin V\) are two distinct destination symbols. Each successor table is a function \(s_b:V\to V\cup\{d_0,d_1\}\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Thus every ordinary vertex has two labelled outgoing arcs, its even arc to \(s_0(v)\) and its odd arc to \(s_1(v)\). These successors may coincide, and self-loops are allowed. The destinations have no outgoing arcs. There are no other edges, weights or choices.

Require that from every ordinary vertex there is a directed path in this switch graph to at least one of the two destinations. A path may use either labelled arc at each vertex for the purpose of checking this condition. It need not follow the token dynamics. This condition is checkable by ordinary reverse graph reachability and guarantees that the actual token process eventually reaches a destination. It does not require that both destinations be reachable from every vertex.

Initially the token is at \(x_0=o\), and every switch bit is zero: \(b_0(v)=0\). If the current position \(x_t\) is a destination, the process stops. Otherwise, writing \(v=x_t\), set
\[x_{t+1}=s_{b_t(v)}(v),\qquad b_{t+1}(v)=1-b_t(v),\]
and leave all other bits unchanged. The successor is selected using the old bit before the bit is flipped. Consequently successive departures from a vertex alternate even, odd, even, odd, starting with even. There is a single token and no player, randomness or external control. The instance is YES if the first reached destination is \(d_1\), and NO if it is \(d_0\).

Encode \(n,o\) and the two length-\(n\) successor tables explicitly using binary integers, with distinguished codes for the two destinations. The input length is \(\Theta(n\log(n+2))\) under this representation, up to fixed delimiters. A graph given by a succinct circuit, a binary multiplicity of initially placed tokens, or an exponentially long switch sequence is not part of this input model. The initial all-zero setting requires no additional table; any fixed initial setting could instead be represented by exchanging the corresponding two successor names.

For an ordinary language rather than a promise problem, reject malformed encodings and well-formed tables failing the reachability condition. Their validity can be checked in polynomial time, so this convention does not alter polynomial-time solvability on the valid instances. The class \(\mathrm P\) means one uniform deterministic program deciding this language on all input strings in a worst-case polynomial number of ordinary bit operations. The program need only output the answer bit. It is not required to list, or simulate, the token's full trajectory.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that this language is in \(\mathrm P\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic decision algorithm, prove correctness on every valid graph and polynomial worst-case bit complexity, and handle invalid encodings according to the stated convention. A negative answer must exclude all such polynomial-time decision algorithms; an exponential example for direct token simulation or for one particular algorithm is insufficient. Polynomial time only for a restricted graph class, subexponential time, a randomized algorithm without a deterministic conversion, and succinctly encoded variants do not answer the exact question. No numerical tolerance applies to the Boolean answer or the complexity bound.

context_blocks.text: The local rule is elementary, but a vertex remembers which of its two arcs should be used next. With n vertices there are 2ⁿ possible switch configurations in addition to the token position. Long deterministic runs therefore do not contradict the small size of the graph. Ordinary reachability ignores these switch settings and does not decide which sink the token actually reaches.

The source gives short verifiable certificates for both answers using switching flows: counts of traversals that obey conservation and alternation. This places the decision problem in NP ∩ coNP. Certificates can establish the outcome without listing an exponentially long trajectory, but their existence does not itself provide a polynomial-time way to find them.

The 2021 algorithm runs in \(2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) time and becomes polynomial when deleting a fixed number of vertices makes the graph acyclic. The former is a general improvement over direct simulation; the latter keeps a structural restriction. Neither is the all-instance polynomial bound asked for here.

The 2025 work gives a bound \(2^{O(k\log^2 n)}\) for treewidth \(k\), which is quasipolynomial, not polynomial, even when \(k\) is fixed. It also relates ARRIVAL to approximate fixed points of contractions in the ℓ₁ metric. The paper explicitly distinguishes polynomially many function evaluations from a polynomial total running time.

The 2026 paper proves polynomial time for binary ladders: simple switch graphs with exactly two vertices at each occupied distance level from the two sinks. Such graphs can frustrate earlier algorithms, so solving them is meaningful progress. The restriction concerns the shortest-distance layers of the graph and is not satisfied by general instances.

A polynomial-time algorithm would settle a basic deterministic process whose YES and NO answers already have efficiently checked evidence. A lower bound excluding all such algorithms would be a major complexity separation; the difficulty of simulating the process is only one part of that question.

cards.title: Closure of UL under complement
cards.formal:
Is unambiguous logarithmic space closed under Boolean complement?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*,\qquad L\in\mathrm{UL}\ \Longrightarrow\ \{0,1\}^*\setminus L\in\mathrm{UL}.\]
Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{coUL}\)? A language is in \(\mathrm{UL}\) if one uniform nondeterministic machine decides it using logarithmic work space and has at most one accepting computation path on every input.

The complementing machine must also have at most one accepting path on every input and logarithmic space with its own fixed constants. The question concerns ordinary uniform machines with no advice or oracle and arbitrary binary input languages, not only planar graph problems.

cards.definitions:
A language is any set of finite binary strings, and \(n=|x|\) denotes input length. Use a nondeterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite control and fixed finite tape alphabets, a two-way read-only input tape with end markers, and finitely many initially blank work tapes. Each transition has at most two choices. The input cannot be modified or used as additional writable memory. Work space is the total number of work-tape cells visited along a computation, measured in bits up to the fixed alphabet factor; the input cells and fixed finite control are not charged as work space.

A machine is logarithmic-space bounded if there is a constant \(c\) such that every computation on every input of length \(n\) visits at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. Use the standard halting convention: some fixed polynomial \(K(n+2)^d\) bounds the number of steps along every computation path, including rejecting paths. The machine and \(c,K,d\) are fixed independently of the input. A polynomial clock fits in logarithmic space; this convention does not add a nonuniform resource.

A computation path is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to an accepting or rejecting halt. Distinct choice histories count as distinct paths even when they later reach the same configuration. Acceptance means that at least one path accepts. The machine decides \(L\) when it accepts exactly the strings of \(L\); all paths on strings outside \(L\) reject.

Unambiguity means at most one accepting path for every binary input. Therefore a yes-instance has exactly one accepting path, while a no-instance has none. There may be many rejecting paths in either case. No probability distribution or bounded-error interpretation of these paths is intended. This is not the stronger requirement that every configuration, or every pair of configurations, be connected by at most one path.

The class \(\mathrm{UL}\) consists of languages decided by some machine satisfying all these conditions. Define \(\mathrm{coUL}=\{\overline L:L\in\mathrm{UL}\}\), where \(\overline L=\{0,1\}^*\setminus L\). Dropping only the unambiguity restriction gives \(\mathrm{NL}\), and restricting to deterministic transitions gives \(\mathrm L\). The usual inclusions are \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\). The known closure \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) makes \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{NL}\) sufficient for the requested closure; no equivalence to that stronger equality is asserted.

The quantifier is over languages: for each language with a qualifying machine, another qualifying machine for its complement must exist. An effective compiler that transforms every description of an unambiguous machine into a complement machine is not additionally required. Nor must the original and complement machines have the same space constant or polynomial clock. A negative answer is a language in \(\mathrm{UL}\) whose complement is not in \(\mathrm{UL}\), with nonmembership excluding all possible unambiguous logarithmic-space machines.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of closure in the declared uniform model. A proof must establish a qualifying complement machine for every language in UL, with exact acceptance, unambiguity on all inputs and logarithmic work space. A refutation must establish a language in UL and prove that its complement has no such machine. Merely complementing nondeterministic logspace while allowing multiple accepting paths, adding advice or an oracle, or settling a restricted family of graph inputs does not meet the full criterion. An oracle separation or a conditional separation alone is not an unconditional refutation.

cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
cards.formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants \(c_{M} \ge  1\) and an integer \(d_{M} \ge  1\) so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair \((x,M(x))\), uses at most \(c_{M} S_{M}(x)\) tape cells, and takes at most \(c_{M} T_{M}(x)^{d_{M}}\) steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here \(S_{M}\) counts total storage including input and output, and \(T_{M}\) is at least the input length, as defined below.
cards.definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. \(S_{M}(x)\) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. \(T_{M}(x)\) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and \(M(x)\), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: Saving the input is necessary when the simulated function is many-to-one: reversible configurations cannot merge different initial inputs into one final configuration. Counting input and output storage prevents free external memory from changing the target.

Known general simulations occupy different parts of the time-space tradeoff. Polynomial-time simulations use more than linear space in general; a simulation with \(O(S)\) space can take exponential time. The requested conjunction does not follow from either result separately.

The compiler formulation makes the simulation uniform across inputs, while allowing machine-dependent constants. It is the polynomial-time, linear-space version requested here, rather than a demand for nearly linear time.

cards.title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
cards.formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
cards.why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

cards.definitions:
A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\). Use uniform finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines, with independent fair random bits, binary input and an accept/reject output. Every random-bit sequence must lead to a halt in time polynomial in input length. Bit operations, random-bit generation and input and output handling count as work. No advice, oracle or quantum register is supplied.

For definiteness, encode a pair by \(\langle x,y\rangle=1^{|x|}0xy\). The initial unary field specifies exactly how many subsequent bits form \(x\), and the rest form \(y\). Strings without such a complete parse are malformed; a pair verifier rejects them deterministically. This is a uniquely decodable, polynomial-size encoding. On well-formed pairs, the time bound is at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\) for fixed positive integers \(C,d\), and the usual polynomial bound applies to all encoded inputs. Let \(a_V(x,y)=\Pr[V(\langle x,y\rangle)=1]\).

The class \(\mathrm{MA}\) consists of languages \(L\) for which there are a verifier \(V\) as above and fixed positive integers \(c,k\), giving a witness bound \(p(n)=c(n+1)^k\), such that
\[x\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ a_V(x,y)\ge2/3,\]
\[x\notin L\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_V(x,y)\le1/3.\]
The witness is chosen before the verifier's random bits are drawn, so it cannot depend on their realized values. When \(x\in L\), the probabilities for other witnesses may be anywhere in \([0,1]\). The language is total as a decision problem: every input is either in \(L\) or in its complement; this is not a promise-MA problem with unclassified inputs.

A language \(A\) is in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) if some uniform randomized polynomial-time machine accepts each \(z\in A\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and each \(z\notin A\) with probability at most \(1/3\). In particular, every input has the required gap. Define the existential operator by
\[L\in\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists A\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \exists c,k\ge1\ \forall x,\quad x\in L\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists y\ \bigl(|y|\le c(|x|+1)^k\ \land\ \langle x,y\rangle\in A\bigr).\]
Here \(c,k\) are integers. The set \(A\) may be assumed to reject malformed pair encodings. The witness bound is a polynomial size bound, not a bound on the cost of finding the witness.

Equivalently, \(L\) has an MA verifier \(W\) that also satisfies
\[\forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^*,\qquad a_W(x,y)\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1].\]
This condition includes witnesses exceeding the chosen length bound; they may be rejected deterministically. It requires one uniform verifier for all \(x,y\), not a separately chosen randomized algorithm for each fixed witness. There is no requirement that a new \(W\) preserve the original verifier's probabilities or use its witness bound.

It follows from these definitions that \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{MA}\). Thus the substantive equality direction is that every language in MA has some globally gapped witness predicate. A negative answer is a language in MA with no such predicate under any polynomial witness bound. Merely presenting one MA verifier with a probability in the gap does not establish that its language lacks a different globally gapped verifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the equality in the uniform, unrelativized language setting. A proof must establish a globally bounded-error witness predicate for every MA language, including exact polynomial runtime and witness-length guarantees. It may change the verifier and witness encoding and need not give an effective conversion between arbitrary machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some MA language has no existential-BPP representation under any allowed verifier and polynomial bound. cards.title: Effective enumeration of BPP
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total computable function \(E\) which, for every index \(i\in\mathbb N\), outputs the finite description of a randomized polynomial-time decision machine \(M_i\), such that
\[\forall i\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\quad\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1],\]
and every language in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) is decided by at least one of these machines?

With \(L_i=\{x:\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\ge2/3\}\), the coverage condition is exactly
\[\{L_i:i\in\mathbb N\}=\mathrm{BPP}.\]
Repeated languages and repeated machine descriptions are allowed. The enumeration must include at least one suitable algorithm for each BPP language; it need not list every bounded-error program. There is no efficiency bound on computing \(E(i)\). Each \(M_i\) may have its own polynomial runtime bound, and the enumerator is not additionally required to output that bound.

source_formulation.text: The existence of an effective enumerable family of algorithms deciding all and only the problems in BPP is still an open question.

cards.why: Polynomial running time can be guaranteed syntactically by a clock, but bounded error is a condition on every possible input. The question asks whether a computably generated family can still capture all feasible randomized decision problems while guaranteeing that condition. A resolution would clarify the relationship between semantic complexity classes, programming formalisms and what arithmetical theories can certify about randomized computation.

cards.definitions:
All languages are subsets of finite binary strings. A randomized decision machine is a finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, initially blank work tapes, a one-bit output and independent fair random bits. It has no oracle, advice or arbitrary real-number operations. Time counts ordinary tape operations, generation of random bits and output writing, in the worst case over random choices.

For each enumerated machine \(M_i\), there must exist positive integers \(C_i,d_i\) such that it halts with a decision bit within \(C_i(n+2)^{d_i}\) bit steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random-bit sequence. These constants may depend on \(i\), but not on the input or random choices. No common polynomial must bound the whole family. The time bounds are existential properties of the emitted programs; no computable method of finding their constants from \(i\), or proof certificate for those constants, is additionally required. An enumeration supplying explicit clocks would be a sufficient special case.

For every finite input, the runtime bound limits the number of coin tosses, so the acceptance probability is a well-defined dyadic rational from a finite probability space. Unused coin bits do not change an output. A machine has bounded error when its acceptance probability never lies strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\). It then decides the unique language whose yes-instances have acceptance probability at least \(2/3\); every no-instance has acceptance probability at most \(1/3\). The gap must hold on every input, including the empty string.

The class \(\mathrm{BPP}\) consists of all languages decided by some randomized polynomial-time machine with this gap. Equivalently, \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) if some such machine satisfies \(\Pr[M(x)=\mathbf 1_L(x)]\ge2/3\) for every \(x\). The class \(\mathrm P\), used in the context, consists of languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time machines. Both classes use worst-case polynomial runtime.

Total computable means that one deterministic Turing machine, given the binary encoding of any nonnegative integer \(i\), halts and returns the finite transition-table code of \(M_i\). It may use arbitrarily large finite time and space as a function of \(i\). No finite or infinite advice sequence and no oracle are allowed. Codes use an ordinary effective finite encoding of machine states, tape symbols and transitions; standard such encodings can be effectively translated without changing the represented machine or its polynomial-time property.

Soundness requires every emitted machine to run in polynomial time and have the displayed gap on every input. Coverage requires that for each \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\), some index \(i\) satisfies \(L=L_i\) on all strings. Neither an index for a given language nor a decision procedure for whether an arbitrary program has the gap is requested. In particular, \(E\) may omit a bounded-error program if it lists another program deciding the same language.

The negative answer excludes every total computable enumeration with these two properties. An inability to enumerate all codes of polynomial-time bounded-error programs is a different assertion: the target only needs an effectively chosen representative family that covers all the languages. No specific logical theory or proof system is prescribed for that family.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such an enumeration. A positive answer must specify a total computable enumerator and prove the polynomial-time and all-input error guarantees for every emitted machine, as well as coverage of every BPP language. The mathematical runtime proof may establish separately quantified constants for each index without providing an algorithm computing them. A negative answer must rule out every such representative-family enumeration, including families whose time bounds are not supplied effectively. Showing that the set of all valid machine codes is undecidable or not computably enumerable does not suffice. An enumeration covering only the languages whose correctness is proved in one selected theory also does not suffice without proving that it covers all of BPP.

context_blocks.text: Section 2 emphasizes the difference between listing all algorithms with a property and listing enough algorithms to cover the same languages. The former code sets can be recursion-theoretically difficult even for deterministic polynomial time, while the latter can have a simple effective enumeration.

The source gives characterizations of BPP in arithmetic and effectively enumerable subclasses based on error guarantees provable in a sound recursively enumerable theory. Its conclusion does not show that one such subclass contains every BPP language.

Proposition 20 shows that P equal to BPP would imply the desired kind of effective characterization. Thus a proof that no covering enumeration exists would in particular separate P from BPP. The reverse implication is not asserted.

The paper proves hardness of recognizing its all-input error condition and gives an enumerable sound-theory subclass containing polynomial identity testing. These results expose the certification issue and supply substantial examples, but neither code-recognition hardness nor one such subclass settles complete language coverage.

cards.title: Polynomial formulas versus linear circuits
cards.formal:
Does there exist a family of total Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for integers \(n\ge1\), such that
\[S(f_n)=O(n)\qquad\text{but}\qquad L(f_n)\notin n^{O(1)}?\]
Here \(S\) is minimum bounded-fan-in De Morgan circuit gate count and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf count. Both are nonuniform and require exact correctness on every input. Precisely, the question asks for one family and a finite constant \(C>0\) satisfying \(S(f_n)\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge1\), while
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N:\quad L(f_n)>n^k.\]
This is the source's absence-of-any-polynomial-upper-bound claim. It does not silently strengthen that claim to a lower bound beating each polynomial at every sufficiently large length.
cards.why: Circuits can reuse intermediate values and formulas must duplicate the computation when it is needed again. This question asks whether reuse can turn a task requiring superpolynomial tree size into a circuit of only linear size. It isolates a fundamental limitation of formulas while allowing the circuit computation to have unrestricted depth.

sentences: The conjecture asks for Boolean functions with linear-size circuits but no polynomial-size formulas.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input nodes for \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and one designated output. Every computational gate is binary AND, binary OR, or unary NOT. Inputs may also supply the constant bits zero and one. Each node carries one bit, which is evaluated by applying its assigned operation to the incoming values. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted, and a gate value can be reused several times. The output can be an input, a constant or a computed gate. Size is the number of computational gates; input and constant nodes and wires are not charged. The circuit must output \(f_n(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). No parity or arbitrary truth-table gate is a primitive, and no random or promise-only correctness is allowed. \(S(f_n)\) is the minimum such size.

A formula is a finite rooted tree with binary AND/OR or unary NOT internal nodes and input-variable or constant leaves. Each occurrence of an input in this tree is separate; an internal computation cannot feed two parent nodes. The size of a formula is the number of variable-leaf occurrences, as in the source. Constant leaves are free; an optimum for a nonconstant function can eliminate constant subformulas. One may equivalently place all NOT operations directly on variables by De Morgan's laws, leaving the leaf count unchanged. Negated and unnegated occurrences of the same variable are each counted. \(L(f_n)\) is the minimum leaf count over formulas computing the function exactly. Constant functions have \(L=0\), and a literal has \(L=1\).

The sequence of functions, and the optimal circuits and formulas at different lengths, need not have an efficiently computable description. In particular this card does not impose an extra polynomial-time evaluator or uniform circuit-generation algorithm on the family. The source's conjecture is stated using its nonuniform size measures. A family with such extra uniformity would also qualify if it has the required sizes.

The same constant \(C\) bounds circuit size at every length. Allowing finitely many exceptions would be equivalent, since increasing \(C\) absorbs them. The formula condition is equivalent to saying that there do not exist constants \(D>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and onset \(N\) with \(L(f_n)\le Dn^k\) for all \(n\ge N\). Thus arbitrarily large violating lengths may depend on the polynomial exponent; the family itself may not. The target asserts no particular exponential or quasipolynomial lower-bound rate.

The two minima compare computations of the same single-output function. Linear circuit size does not bound circuit depth by a logarithm. A size separation using unbounded-fan-in threshold gates, only monotone formulas, or a growing number of outputs is a different statement.

The existence claim is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\subsetneq\mathrm{P/poly}\) for nonuniform Boolean circuit families. Here \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) means \(S(f_n)\le a(n+1)^b\) for some fixed positive integers \(a,b\), and \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) means a family of binary De Morgan circuits of depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for one constant \(d\); such circuits can be taken polynomial in size. No uniform generation is required in either class. Polynomial-size formulas and logarithmic-depth circuits are equivalent by formula balancing and expansion of a bounded-depth circuit into a tree.

The restriction to linear circuit size does not change this family-existence question. A separating polynomial-size family can be regarded, at lengths \(N_n=a(n+1)^b\), as a function of \(N_n\) variables that ignores the extra variables; at other lengths set the function to a constant. The circuit bound becomes linear, whereas a polynomial formula bound in \(N_n\) would give a polynomial formula bound in \(n\). This is a comparison of nonuniform families and retains the arbitrarily-large-length quantifiers. Conversely, a linear-size family is already in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). Thus an answer to the equality question has the opposite Boolean polarity from the separation question in this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed family-existence claim. A positive answer must specify or mathematically establish the existence of one family satisfying both the single linear circuit bound and failure of every polynomial formula bound. A nonconstructive family can qualify; no efficient generator is part of the target. A negative answer must show that every family with a uniform linear circuit-size constant has some polynomial formula-size bound, whose exponent and coefficient may depend on that family. Proving only one fixed polynomial separation, even with a large exponent, or refuting one candidate family does not settle the question.

There is no additional space restriction on \(D\). This card uses the single-decider \(2^{o(n)}\) meaning of subexponential time, matching the explicit time scale discussed in the source. The source question is about arbitrary two-way random-tape access, even though the paper’s main advice theorem concerns a bounded number of one-way passes.

sentences: This question concerns randomized logspace algorithms that can reread a fixed polynomial-length random tape in either direction.
It asks whether every language they decide has a uniform exact deterministic algorithm whose worst-case runtime has an exponent sublinear in input length.

cards.definitions:
Inputs are finite binary strings \(x\), with length \(n\). A randomized machine is a uniform finite-program multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, a read-only random tape and a fixed number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input and random heads may each move one cell left or right, or stay in place, at a step; their boundaries are marked and cannot be crossed. The input may be reread without restriction.

For fixed positive integers \(a,b,c,d\) depending only on the machine, the random tape holds
\[r(n)=a(n+1)^b\]
bits sampled uniformly and independently at the start of the run, and the total work-tape storage is at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits on every input and every random string. Padding the random tape by unused random bits is allowed. A reread of a random cell returns its original sampled bit; it does not toss a new coin. The read-only input and random tapes do not count as writable work space. Any work-tape storage used for counters, remembered bits or bookkeeping does count. There is no additional stream of fresh randomness, writable uncharged auxiliary tape, advice or external oracle.

The machine halts with a one-bit accept/reject answer within \(d(n+1)^d\) steps for every random tape. This is a worst-case polynomial clock, not an expected-time convention. Polynomial time also bounds the number of changes of direction or complete passes. Head movements, tape operations and reading a random bit each cost a machine step. The algorithm may inspect random positions adaptively; no bound by a fixed number of sweeps is imposed.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{2\text{-}wayBPL}\) if some such machine \(M\) satisfies
\[\forall x\in L,\quad\Pr_{r\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{r(|x|)})}[M(x;r)=1]\ge2/3,\]
\[\forall x\notin L,\quad\Pr_{r\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{r(|x|)})}[M(x;r)=1]\le1/3.\]
The random-string variable in these displays is a full tape content. Correctness is required for every input separately, and all binary strings are either yes- or no-instances; there is no promise gap in the input domain. The newer notation \(\mathrm{BP}\!\cdot\!\mathrm L\) in the cited 2024 paper refers to this persistent, rereadable randomness model for decision languages. Ordinary BPL instead restricts the random tape to one-way access.

The deterministic simulator is a uniform multitape Turing decider with no random tape, advice or oracle. It must output \(1\) exactly on \(L\) and halt on every binary input. Set
\[T_D(n)=\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\operatorname{time}_D(x).\]
The required limit is equivalently: for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(N_\varepsilon\) such that \(T_D(n)\le2^{\varepsilon n}\) for all \(n\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same \(D\) must satisfy all these bounds. It may depend on \(L\), as may the thresholds; the assertion does not require an effective compiler from descriptions of randomized machines.

The criterion is not merely a running time \(2^{n^k}\) for some fixed \(k\), nor a fixed exponential saving \(2^{0.99n}\). It also does not demand the stronger family of bounds \(2^{n^\varepsilon}\) for every positive \(\varepsilon\). The selected convention is explicitly the limit above. A refutation is a language in the stated randomized class for which every correct deterministic decider fails that limit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the containment under the specified tape and runtime conventions. A proof must establish one exact deterministic decider of sublinear-exponent worst-case time for every language in the class. It need not preserve the logarithmic space bound or effectively transform arbitrary randomized machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some language in the class has no deterministic decider meeting the displayed limit. A simulation with advice, a bound only for restricted random-tape movements, correctness on most inputs or a conditional hardness-to-randomness implication alone is insufficient.

cards.title: Doubly efficient \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
cards.formal: For every uniform deterministic polynomial-space decider \(M\) and every time-constructible bound \(T(n)\ge n+2\) on its running time, does the language \(L(M)\) have a uniform classical single-prover interactive proof with a verifier running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time and an honest prover running in \(\operatorname{poly}(T(n))\) total time, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) against every cheating prover? The quantifier covers the full time range, rather than only \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\).
cards.why: The class equality IP = PSPACE says that polynomial space can be verified efficiently, but does not by itself control the cost of generating the proof relative to the original computation. The target asks whether that prover overhead can always be polynomial while retaining soundness against an unlimited adversary.

cards.definitions:
Fix the standard bit-cost model of deterministic multitape Turing machines with a read-only binary input tape. A decider halts and accepts or rejects on every binary input. For each fixed \(M\), there is a polynomial \(q\) such that on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), \(M\) uses at most \(q(n+2)\) work-tape cells and takes at most \(T(n)\) steps. The same machine must satisfy both bounds. Here \(T:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\) is time-constructible in the following convention: some fixed deterministic machine, on unary input \(1^n\), outputs the binary representation of \(T(n)\) within \(K T(n)\) steps for a constant \(K\). The requirement \(T(n)\ge n+2\) merely absorbs bounded lengths. Define \(L(M)=\{x:M\text{ accepts }x\}\).

An interactive proof consists of two fixed finite programs, an honest prover \(P\) and a verifier \(V\), which both receive only the common input \(x\) and exchange finite binary messages. They may use independent private fair random bits. A protocol may expose verifier randomness through its messages, but public coins and perfect completeness are not extra requirements. The machines know their fixed protocol and may incorporate the fixed descriptions of \(M\) and a constructor for \(T\). They receive no advice depending on input length, trusted preprocessing, shared secret, additional witness, oracle, or separately supplied value of \(T(n)\).

For each fixed \(M,T\), there must be constants \(C,a,b\ge1\) and one such pair \(P,V\), all independent of \(n,x\), satisfying these bounds for every input. The verifier's total number of bit operations is at most \(C(n+2)^a\), on every random tape and against every possible sequence of prover messages. It accepts or rejects within that bound. The total number of messages, all transmitted or read message bits and verifier random bits are charged to this bound; malformed or oversized messages may be rejected. The honest prover's total number of bit operations during an interaction with \(V\) is at most \(C(T(n)+2)^b\), on every choice of both random tapes, including inputs outside the language. All input-dependent preprocessing, message generation and communication are included. No separate restriction to polynomial prover space is imposed.

Completeness requires
\[
\Pr[\langle P,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3
\quad\text{for every }x\in L(M),
\]
where the probability is over both machines' independent random bits. Soundness requires, for every \(x\notin L(M)\) and every cheating strategy \(P^*\),
\[
\Pr[\langle P^*,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\le1/3.
\]
A cheating strategy can depend arbitrarily on \(x\) and its visible transcript and can perform unlimited computation; it has no access to unexposed verifier randomness. It may be randomized, with its private randomness independent of the verifier's. There is only one prover, and no computational assumption restricts soundness.

The quantifier order is: for every fixed pair \(M,T\) satisfying the time and polynomial-space premises, there exist \(P,V,C,a,b\) that work for all inputs and lengths. No algorithm transforming descriptions of \(M,T\) into protocols is additionally demanded. The prover bound refers to the specified \(T(n)\), not to an unrestricted exponential in the space bound. The verifier bound remains polynomial in the original input length even when \(T\) is superquasipolynomial.

cards.title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
cards.formal: Put \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\). For \(0\le p<1/2\), let \(\mathcal C_p(n)\) be the finite noisy circuits defined below. Define reliable computation at noise \(p\) by \[\operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff \exists\delta\in(0,1/2]\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\ \exists C\in\mathcal C_p(n)\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\Pr[C(x)=f(x)]\ge1/2+\delta.\] Is the following proposition true? \[\forall p\in[0,1/2):\quad \operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff p<\beta.\] In particular, the proposition includes impossibility at \(p=\beta\).
cards.definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with labeled input sources \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), noiseless constant sources \(0,1\), and one designated output wire. A computational gate has one or two ordered input wires and an arbitrary fixed Boolean truth table on those bits. Wires may connect a source or an earlier gate to any number of later gates; both inputs of a gate may come from the same predecessor. There are no other gates, external coins, auxiliary inputs, or oracle operations. A gate-free output is allowed to read one source directly.

For every computational gate \(v\), independently sample \(Z_v\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Z_v=1]=p\). Evaluate the DAG in topological order. If the gate truth table applied to its received bits gives \(b\), its actual value is \(b\mathbin{\oplus}Z_v\), where \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Every outgoing wire carries this same actual value. All gate failures are mutually independent and independent of the input; wire values sharing a predecessor need not be independent. Input sources and wires are perfect. All computational gates, including NOT and any output gate, have exactly the same flip probability \(p\); no noiseless output decoder is supplied.

The probability in the target is only over this finite product of gate-failure distributions, for a fixed input \(x\). The circuit and its wiring and truth tables may depend on the real parameter \(p\), the integer \(n\), and the entire function \(f\), but not on the actual input \(x\) or realized failures. The advantage \(\delta\) may depend on \(p\), but is chosen before \(n\) and \(f\). Circuit size, depth and construction time are unrestricted, and no uniform algorithm constructing the circuits is required. A formula is the special case where every computational gate has at most one outgoing wire; an input variable can still occur on multiple leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal equivalence or its logical negation, in the specified independent gate-flip model. The same positive advantage must work for every input length and every Boolean function at each fixed noise level. The boundary \(p=\beta\) is part of the claim. A theorem only for formulas, only for a restricted gate basis, or with a separate noiseless decoder does not decide this circuit proposition. A negative resolution of reliable computation must rule out all finite circuit sizes; failure of one construction is insufficient.
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

importance.reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.

context_blocks.text: The task concerns whether arbitrary computation remains possible at all under local errors, even when unlimited redundancy is permitted. The target keeps a positive correctness margin independent of the function and its number of inputs. It is not a circuit-size overhead problem or an average over randomly chosen inputs.

Unger’s theorem gives the sharp formula boundary \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\), including failure of universal reliable computation at equality, and explicitly conjectures the extension to circuits. Formulas cannot reuse an intermediate noisy gate value; circuits can, so independent gate failures do not make the received signals independent. The positive formula result below \(\beta\) also provides circuits.

The later formulation of reliable computation in Definition 2.1 of Shutty, Wootters and Hayden uses one advantage for all Boolean functions, as here. Their survey distinguishes the symmetric two-input formula threshold from the known general-circuit upper bound \(1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2})\). Their main asymmetric model permits gate-dependent errors, including noiseless XOR, and its proposed circuit extension is conditional. Those statements do not settle the identical-noise circuit claim.

The July 2025 essay revisits established circuit-noise bounds and discusses majority gates of higher arity. Its stated scope does not supply the missing exact threshold for arbitrary two-input circuits.

cards.title: Polynomial-size closure of d-DNNF under negation
cards.formal:
Do constants \(c>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, for every finite variable set \(X\) and every d-DNNF circuit \(C\) over \(X\), there is a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over \(X\) with
\[s(D)\le c\bigl(s(C)+1\bigr)^k\quad\text{and}\quad\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\ f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The constants are universal: they cannot depend on \(X\), \(C\) or its Boolean function. No algorithm, uniformity or bound on the time needed to find \(D\) is required. Its internal decompositions may differ from those of \(C\), with no global variable-tree restriction on either circuit.
cards.definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

The output uses only variables of \(X\), interpreted on the same coordinates, with no auxiliary variables or existential projection. It need not mention every variable. The size counts the complete circuit rather than an implicit description or an oracle for evaluating it. The target is nonconstructive representational closure with polynomial overhead, not closure as a set of Boolean functions alone.

The exact negation of the claim is that for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some finite \(X\) and some d-DNNF \(C\) have the property that every d-DNNF \(D\) computing its complement satisfies \(s(D)>c(s(C)+1)^k\). This need not be witnessed by one fixed input circuit defeating all polynomials, or by an efficiently constructible family. A uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm would imply the size bound; the converse is not part of this statement.

A refutation must establish the quantified superpolynomial obstruction for general output d-DNNFs. A lower bound that only excludes structured outputs, a particular decomposition or a particular algorithm is insufficient. Computational difficulty in finding a complement alone also does not refute existence of a small complement.
